threat_assessment: Your problem is that Dragons cannot pretend to be a 3/3 — perceived threat runs ahead of actual threat for the first five turns, exactly when the goldfish says you are weakest: mean available mana 4.947 and 1.536 bodies at turn 6, commander cast by turn 6 in 0.0% of runs, mean cast turn 8.989. The table sees a five-colour Ur-Dragon deck and prices in the ending; you have to make them mis-time the response. So for turns 1-4 you are the control/value seat (strategic_frame role_assignment), and your job is to look like mana and lands: rocks, Farseek, Nature's Lore, Dragon's Hoard, Urza's Incubator draw almost no interaction on their own. The pieces that actually flip your table read are the payoff layer, not the bodies — Dragon Tempest at two mana, Temur Ascendancy at three. Experienced tables know verified line 001 (Tempest plus Ancient Gold Dragon is a table-scale damage burst) and know Miirym doubles everything (verified stack 002), so the moment Tempest or Ascendancy resolves alongside untapped mana and cards in hand, you are archenemy regardless of your board. Sequence accordingly: deploy the cheap payoff the same turn you deploy Dragons into it, not a turn early as an invitation. The known-card signals that flip the table hardest, in order: Tiamat resolving (five cards to hand is a public countdown), Hellkite Courser (everyone knows what it fetches), and any haste enabler with five-plus mana up. When to embrace it: the pivot window (strategy:multiplayer.pivot-window) is a haste enabler on board plus two-to-three deployable Dragons in one turn — and the goldfish says you rarely get a second window (protection held by turn 6 in 66.4% of games, reducer-plus-ramp by turn 6 in only 29.4%), so when you commit, commit through held protection and count all three opponents' open mana first. One more signal discipline note: casting protection (Teferi's Protection, Heroic Intervention) proactively before anyone has threatened you telegraphs the big turn a full rotation early. Hold it; the frame's math says one wrath per game is near-certain, and your protection package is exactly the tool that converts their reset into your pivot.
matchups: Sweeper control (your defining matchup): they own the mid-game reset, and your deck folds bodies, payoffs, and draw into one wrath-vulnerable pile — 24 threat:body entries with the card advantage sitting on permanents. Commit exactly what wins before the wrath and no more, in waves. Your two rebuild aces are Patriarch's Bidding (all your Dragons return; their non-typal yard returns nothing comparable) and Haven of the Spirit Dragon, and your enchantment layer (Temur Ascendancy, Garruk's Uprising, Dragon Tempest) survives creature sweepers, so your post-wrath wave is hasty and draws — the wrath is often your pivot point, not theirs. Goldfish says you hold protection by turn 6 in 66.4% of games; when you do, Heroic Intervention and Flawless Maneuver (free with a commander) flip a destroy-based sweep into a blowout, but neither beats exile or bounce — read which wrath the Esper deck actually plays. Stax/tax: taxes punish spell velocity, and you cast few, huge, double-discounted spells — Eminence plus Urza's Incubator plus Herald's Horn eat Thalia effects for breakfast, and your six spells-only sources (Haven, Rivaz, Sarkhan Fireblood, Unclaimed Territory, Maelstrom, Klauth) keep working because they cast spells; just remember they cannot pay activated abilities at all (deck-facts restricted_mana). Race an assembling lock; you are the beatdown there. Aggro: you are the control — you cannot race (0 commander casts by turn 6), so trade with big blockers, and note Crux of Fate can wipe only the non-Dragons while Blasphemous Act is your reset button. Turn the corner the moment you stabilize. Combo: their inevitability beats your 8.989-turn clock. Your only relevant answers are Counterspell, Swan Song, Dovin's Veto, and An Offer You Can't Refuse — four cards in 66 spells, so answer economy is everything: spend them exclusively on game-ending spells, never on value pieces. Graveyard hate: it hurts more than people expect — Bidding and Haven are your sweeper-matchup engine, and Rivaz recasts from the yard, so a Rest in Peace quietly deletes your rebuild plan; against it, shift to the hold-and-wave line and lean harder on protection. One sideboard note: the Savage Ventmaw plus Aggravated Assault extra-combat loop is verified real and unbounded (stack 003), but Assault lives in the sideboard — that line is live only if the swap is made, and making it raises what your table should expect from you.
how_it_wins:
Start by unlearning the obvious read: The Ur-Dragon is not the plan. The goldfish simulator (seed 42, 10,000 iterations, conservative model — cost reducers not simulated) puts his mean cast on turn 8.989, with a 0% cast-by-turn-6 rate and a cast at all by turn 10 in just 13.5% of runs. What IS the plan is his Eminence line, which works from the command zone starting on turn zero: every other Dragon spell you cast costs {1} less, all game, without him ever leaving home. Stack that with Dragonlord's Servant, Dragonspeaker Shaman, Herald's Horn, and Urza's Incubator and a nine-drop curve plays like a six-drop curve — which is the entire architectural bet this deck makes.

The engine that actually kills people is the enters-and-attacks payoff layer. Dragon Tempest, Scourge of Valkas, and Terror of the Peaks turn each Dragon entering into targeted damage; Garruk's Uprising and Temur Ascendancy turn big bodies into cards; Miirym, Sentinel Wyrm turns every nontoken Dragon into two. This is a critical-mass deck: below the threshold you have undersized, expensive bodies, and past it every new Dragon draws, burns, and copies itself. The verified stacks show the payoff math — one Ancient Gold Dragon connection under Dragon Tempest produced fifteen tokens and up to 255 points of divisible damage (stack 001), and a single Lathliss cast under Miirym plus Panharmonicon produced two extra Lathlisses and 64 damage across twelve triggers (stack 002).

Your seat for the first five turns is control-slash-value, whether you like it or not: the deck averages 4.95 available mana and 1.54 bodies at turn 6, so it loses every early race. Trade with big blockers, hold the counterspells for spells that actually end the game, and ramp toward the pivot. The pivot window is concrete: a haste enabler on the table (Dragon Tempest or Temur Ascendancy) plus two or three Dragons deployable in one turn — or Tiamat or the commander resolving. That turn you flip to beatdown, and every passive turn afterward is a free draw step for three opponents. Deploy in waves rather than all at once: across a four-player game a wrath is near-certain, and this deck keeps all its card advantage on permanents. The protection package — Teferi's Protection, Heroic Intervention, Flawless Maneuver, Eerie Interlude, plus Patriarch's Bidding as the rebuild — is held by turn 6 in 66% of games; hold one before you commit the wave.

One mana warning the deck-facts brief flags explicitly: six of your sources — Haven of the Spirit Dragon, Maelstrom of the Spirit Dragon, Unclaimed Territory, Rivaz of the Claw, Sarkhan, Fireblood, and Klauth's attack mana — are restricted to casting spells. An activated ability is not a spell, so none of that mana can ever pay for Dragon's Hoard draws, Lathliss pumps, or Haven's own recursion. It accelerates casting Dragons and nothing else; count your unrestricted mana separately when planning an ability-heavy turn.

combo_lines.001: The deck's signature burst, verified step by step against the June 19, 2026 comprehensive rules. The scene: Dragon Tempest, Ancient Gold Dragon, and Miirym on your battlefield, and Ancient Gold Dragon has just dealt combat damage to a 30-life opponent — the d20 comes up 15. Fifteen 1/1 Faerie Dragon tokens enter at once, and every instinct about this board gets tested: Miirym copies none of them (her trigger reads 'nontoken', and the checker confirmed tokens never qualify), but Dragon Tempest sees all fifteen, granting haste and triggering its damage ability fifteen separate times. Each trigger reads the battlefield at resolution — seventeen Dragons — so each one deals 17 to an independently chosen target, with priority passing between resolutions. That is up to 255 damage on offer; the 30-life opponent dies to the second trigger pointed their way, their 4/4 leaves the game with them, and any triggers still aimed at either fizzle. The resolution below walks every window.
combo_lines.002: The question this stack settles: when Lathliss, Dragon Queen resolves under Miirym, Sentinel Wyrm, Panharmonicon, Terror of the Peaks, and Dragon Tempest, what exactly happens? The checker-verified answer is a cascade with a precise shape. Panharmonicon doubles every trigger in the chain, because every one of them is caused by a creature entering — so Miirym triggers twice and you get two nonlegendary 6/6 Lathliss copies, each of which re-triggers the whole payoff layer as it enters. The final tally from one five-mana cast: two extra Lathlisses and 64 damage in twelve separately targeted instances — 36 from Terror of the Peaks, 28 from Dragon Tempest with optimal trigger ordering. Just as important is why it stops: every 'nontoken' clause excludes the copies' own entries, which is what keeps the loop finite and the deck at its bracket. In the verified scenario the 32-life opponent dies outright.
combo_lines.003: Read this one with the sideboard in hand: Aggravated Assault is NOT in the 99. This stack was run precisely because the combo database has claimed lines this pipeline later refuted, and the sideboard analysis needed a verdict before recommending the swap. The verdict: real. Savage Ventmaw's attack trigger adds {R}{R}{R}{G}{G}{G} that persists through steps and phases; in the postcombat main phase that pays Aggravated Assault's {3}{R}{R} with {R} left over, untapping your team and buying another combat — a self-sustaining, unbounded loop netting one mana per cycle. On the verified board Old Gnawbone extends it, minting Treasures whenever your fliers connect, and the 40-life opponent dies on the fourth combat. But this line only exists after you make the sideboard's bracket-conditional swap (Aggravated Assault in, Crucible of Fire out), and making it moves the computed bracket floor from 3 to 4. It is a verified weapon the sideboard unlocks — bring it to tables that agreed to it.

card_roles.The Ur-Dragon: The engine that never needs to be cast: Eminence discounts every other Dragon spell from the command zone all game. When he does arrive (goldfish mean: turn 9), his attack trigger — a card per attacking Dragon plus a free permanent from hand — is the payoff mode, and he deserves protection cover that turn because a {2}-taxed recast of nine mana is close to unpayable.
card_roles.Tiamat: The five-card refill: cast from hand, she tutors up to five differently named Dragons. She is the alternate top-end that turns one resolved spell into the rest of the game — and a prime target for the counterspells you should expect.
card_roles.Dragon Tempest: The keystone enchantment and star of verified stacks 001 and 003's supporting cast: haste for every flier entering, plus X damage per Dragon entering where X is your Dragon count. It converts deployment into removal and reach — land it before the wave, not after.
card_roles.Scourge of Valkas: Dragon Tempest's twin on a body: every Dragon entering (itself included) deals damage equal to your Dragon count. Redundancy in the deck's core damage engine — with both down, every Dragon enters as a two-bolt salvo.
card_roles.Terror of the Peaks: The enters-payoff that scales with power instead of count — each creature you play deals its power to any target, and the 3-life targeting tax protects it. In verified stack 002 it accounted for 36 of the 64 damage from a single Lathliss cast.
card_roles.Miirym, Sentinel Wyrm: Every nontoken Dragon you play arrives twice — the copy is nonlegendary, so even Dragonlords double up. Ward {2} buys her time, and under Panharmonicon (verified stack 002) she triggers twice per Dragon. She is the multiplier the whole payoff layer feeds on.
card_roles.Panharmonicon: Doubles every enters-trigger the engine produces — Miirym, Tempest, Valkas, Terror, Garruk's Uprising, Temur Ascendancy. Stack 002 verified the full cascade: it applies to every trigger caused by a creature entering, turning one Dragon cast into a dozen resolutions.
card_roles.Lathliss, Dragon Queen: Each nontoken Dragon brings a 5/5 token friend, and her {1}{R} pump is a mana sink — though note the spells-only Dragon mana cannot pay for it. In stack 002 one Lathliss cast under the full engine dealt 64 damage.
card_roles.Utvara Hellkite: The attack-side token engine: every attacking Dragon makes a 6/6 flier. Two turns of a modest board snowballs past any answer short of a wrath.
card_roles.Ancient Gold Dragon: The burst enabler of verified stack 001: combat damage to a player rolls a d20 and makes that many 1/1 Faerie Dragons — each one a Dragon entering for Tempest and Valkas. A mid-roll connection is routinely lethal through the payoff layer.
card_roles.Old Gnawbone: Combat-to-mana conversion: Treasures equal to combat damage your creatures deal to players. One connected wave funds the next one — and in verified stack 003's board it sustains the Aggravated Assault loop. A duplicate copy sits in the sideboard as a spare, not an option.
card_roles.Goldspan Dragon: Haste, a Treasure on attack or when targeted, and doubled Treasure output. Five mana that immediately starts paying you back, and the Treasure clause makes every Gnawbone and Cavern-Hoard trigger twice as rich.
card_roles.Savage Ventmaw: Six mana on attack that survives through the whole turn — enough to cast a post-combat Dragon every swing, and (stack 003, verified) exactly enough to go infinite with the sideboard's Aggravated Assault. Note the mana is spendable on anything, unlike the deck's spells-only sources.
card_roles.Klauth, Unrivaled Ancient: Attack-mana that scales with your whole team's power — but it is spells-only mana (deck-facts flags it): it casts your hand, and cannot pay a single activated ability. With a real board he casts two Dragons per combat.
card_roles.Cavern-Hoard Dragon: Costs {X} less for the greatest number of artifacts an opponent controls — often four or five mana at a Treasure-heavy table — with haste, trample, and Treasures per artifact the defender controls on connection. Aim it at the artifact player.
card_roles.Drakuseth, Maw of Flames: Ten damage split across three targets every attack, before blockers matter. The deck's cleanest answer to opposing boards short of a sweeper — a removal spell that attacks.
card_roles.Thrakkus the Butcher: Doubles the power of every Dragon you control when he attacks. With even three Dragons out that is a lethality check for the whole table; with Garruk's Uprising granting trample, the math usually ends games.
card_roles.Atarka, World Render: Every attacking Dragon gains double strike. Pairs with Thrakkus for quadruple effective power, and turns The Ur-Dragon's own attack into 20 commander damage.
card_roles.Scourge of the Throne: Dethrone plus a free extra combat when it attacks the life leader — the deck's maindeck extra-combat effect. The second-combat dethrone recheck is an open rules question flagged for a future stack scenario; until then, plan the first combat to be the one that counts.
card_roles.Dragonlord Dromoka: Uncounterable, lifelink, and opponents cannot cast spells during your turn — she makes your pivot turn consequence-free. Sequence her first on the turn you commit the wave; everything after her resolves in peace.
card_roles.Dragonlord Kolaghan: A haste anthem on a 6/5 flier: your whole board attacks the turn it lands. The 10-life graveyard clause is incidental; the haste is the payload — it opens the pivot window all by herself.
card_roles.Witherbloom, the Balancer: Affinity for creatures makes her a routine 4-to-6-mana 6/6, and she grants your instants and sorceries the same discount — a late-game Rishkar's Expertise or Return of the Wildspeaker for one or two mana.
card_roles.Hellkite Courser: The commander loan: his enters-trigger puts The Ur-Dragon onto the battlefield from the command zone with haste for one attack — the draw-and-free-permanent trigger without paying nine, dodging the goldfish math entirely. Return him at end step and Eminence keeps running.
card_roles.Breaching Dragonstorm: Enters-trigger exiles to the first nonland card and casts it free if it costs 8 or less — and any Dragon entering bounces it to your hand to do it again. In this curve, 'a free haymaker per rebuy' is the honest description.
card_roles.Encroaching Dragonstorm: Two basics onto the battlefield, then it bounces home whenever a Dragon enters — repeatable ramp stapled to the deck's core action. A sideboard duplicate exists purely as a spare.
card_roles.Roiling Dragonstorm: Loot two on entry, bounce home when a Dragon enters, recast, repeat. The cheap card-flow engine the payoff layer keeps recycling.
card_roles.Dragonback Assault: A 3-damage board shock on entry, then a 4/4 Dragon token per land drop — a wrath-insurance engine that rebuilds your board off the resource you were spending anyway.
card_roles.Dracogenesis: Eight mana, then every Dragon spell is free. The most telegraphed card in the deck and the most explosive: untapping with it usually empties your hand into the payoff layer in one turn.
card_roles.Temur Ascendancy: Haste for the team plus a card for every power-4+ creature entering — half the pivot trigger and a third of the draw layer in one three-pip enchantment. The colour ask (G/U/R) is real; check your sources.
card_roles.Garruk's Uprising: Trample for everyone and a card per big creature entering — the green half of the on-board draw engine. Notably, the obsolescence index lists it as the modern replacement for Temur Ascendancy's draw mode; this deck simply runs both.
card_roles.Return of the Wildspeaker: Draw equal to your biggest non-Human's power — routinely five to eight cards at instant speed — or a +3/+3 team pump for the lethal push. The modal flexibility is the point: refill after a wrath, or close through blockers.
card_roles.Rishkar's Expertise: Draw equal to your biggest creature's power, then cast a five-or-less spell free. The single biggest refill in the deck; sequence it after your fattest Dragon and before your next wave.
card_roles.Rivaz of the Claw: Two spells-only Dragon mana a turn (deck-facts: it cannot pay abilities), plus one Dragon creature cast from your graveyard each turn — mana rock and recursion engine in one three-drop with menace.
card_roles.Sarkhan, Fireblood: Loot or two Dragons-only mana every turn, with an ultimate that makes four 5/5 fliers. His mana is spells-only — it casts Dragons and nothing else — but that is exactly the job.
card_roles.Dragonlord's Servant: The floor of the discount stack: Dragon spells cost {1} less. The sideboard analysis marks this as the cut for Korlessa — the deck's seventh cost-reduction effect is worth less than a second draw engine.
card_roles.Dragonspeaker Shaman: Dragon spells cost {2} less — with Eminence, your six-drops cost three. The deepest single discount in the deck and a priority early play; expect it to eat removal, and be glad it drew it away from the payoffs.
card_roles.Herald's Horn: Names Dragons: {1} off every Dragon spell plus a free extra card whenever the top of your library is a Dragon. Discount and card advantage in one rock-shaped package.
card_roles.Urza's Incubator: The biggest pure discount: Dragon spells cost {2} less, stacking with Eminence for {3} total. The goldfish model treats cost reducers as the deck's real curve fixer — this is the best of them.
card_roles.Crucible of Fire: +3/+3 for the team — but the sideboard analysis names it the cut for Aggravated Assault at bracket-4 tables: the deck wins on triggers (Tempest, Terror, Valkas), not on making oversized fliers slightly more oversized.
card_roles.Sol Ring: Two colorless mana on turn one; the fastest route to a turn-3 discount creature or turn-4 payoff enchantment.
card_roles.Arcane Signet: Any commander colour for two — in a five-colour deck this is fixing first, acceleration second.
card_roles.Chromatic Lantern: Every land taps for any colour — the single card that retires the five-colour mana problem, which deck-facts shows is real (every colour is short on lands alone).
card_roles.Dragon's Hoard: Any-colour rock that banks a gold counter per Dragon entering, cashed for cards. Remember: the spells-only Dragon mana cannot pay its draw activation — use lands and rocks for that.
card_roles.Relic of Legends: Any-colour rock with a second mode: tap an untapped legendary creature for another any-colour mana. Fifteen legendary permanents in this deck make the second line live surprisingly often.
card_roles.Mox Jasper: Zero-mana, any-colour — once you control a Dragon. Dead on turn one, excellent from the mid-game on; play it whenever it comes down, it costs nothing.
card_roles.Farseek: Two-mana ramp that finds any of the four non-Forest shock/battle land types — in this manabase it is a colour-fixing scalpel, not just a land.
card_roles.Nature's Lore: A Forest onto the battlefield untapped — which in this deck includes Breeding Pool, Stomping Ground, Overgrown Tomb, and the triomes' Forest types. Best two-mana ramp spell in the list.
card_roles.Skyshroud Claim: Two Forests onto the battlefield untapped — the four-mana play that jumps you from turn 4 to a turn-5 discounted haymaker. The obsolescence index lists Farseek and Nature's Lore as its modern peers; the deck runs all three because the redundancy is the point.
card_roles.Counterspell: One of four counters guarding a slow deck's pivot: per the strategic frame, hold it for the spell that ends the game, not the value piece.
card_roles.Swan Song: One mana, counters the enchantment, instant, or sorcery that kills the table; the 2/2 Bird is a bargain against a game-ending spell.
card_roles.An Offer You Can't Refuse: One-mana noncreature counter that gifts two Treasures — the sideboard analysis marks it the cut for Deflecting Swat, which protects the same spells for free without ramping the opponent you just answered.
card_roles.Dovin's Veto: The uncounterable counter — the one you hold for the counter-war over your Tiamat or their wincon.
card_roles.Swords to Plowshares: The cleanest single-target answer in the game: exile the commander or the combo piece that threatens your long game.
card_roles.Generous Gift: Destroy any permanent — land, enchantment, planeswalker, problem — for three mana; a 3/3 Elephant is nothing to a table full of Dragons.
card_roles.Chaos Warp: The catch-all for what red-green-heavy decks normally can't touch: shuffle away any permanent at instant speed and gamble on the reveal.
card_roles.Blasphemous Act: Thirteen damage to everything, usually for one or two mana at a full table. Your Dragons die too — sequence it before the wave, not after, or pair it with an indestructible effect.
card_roles.Crux of Fate: The one-sided mode is why it's here: destroy all non-Dragon creatures and keep your entire board. The other mode answers opposing Dragon decks.
card_roles.Boros Charm: The mode that matters is 'permanents you control gain indestructible' — a one-card answer to the wrath that ruins critical-mass decks. Four damage and double strike are the bonus modes.
card_roles.Teferi's Protection: The gold standard of wrath insurance: life locked, protection from everything, board phased out. The strategic frame's advice: save it for the turn The Ur-Dragon finally lands.
card_roles.Heroic Intervention: Two mana, hexproof and indestructible for everything — the cheapest full-board answer to both wraths and targeted removal.
card_roles.Flawless Maneuver: Free with your commander out — which, thanks to Eminence being the plan, means 'free the turn it matters most'. Indestructible for the team through the wrath.
card_roles.Eerie Interlude: Blink your board past a sweeper — and every Dragon returning at end step re-triggers the entire enters-payoff layer. Defence that doubles as a second wave.
card_roles.Patriarch's Bidding: The rebuild: every Dragon in your graveyard returns to play at once — and each one re-triggers Tempest, Valkas, Terror, and Miirym. The card that turns an opposing wrath into your best turn. Mind the {B}{B}: black is the deck's thinnest colour on lands.
card_roles.Sarkhan's Triumph: Three mana, any Dragon to hand at instant speed — fetch the engine piece the board is missing: Miirym for mass, Dromoka for safety, Ancient Gold Dragon for the verified kill.
card_roles.Worldly Tutor: One mana for any creature on top of your library — with Korlessa promoted from the sideboard, 'on top' becomes 'castable'. Usually finds Miirym or the Dragon your combat math needs.
card_roles.Enlightened Tutor: One mana for any artifact or enchantment on top: Dragon Tempest, Panharmonicon, Urza's Incubator, or the Dracogenesis endgame. The cheapest way to assemble the verified engines on schedule.
card_roles.Haven of the Spirit Dragon: Any colour for Dragon creature spells only (deck-facts: this mana can never pay an activated ability, including its own), plus a sacrifice mode that rebuys a dead Dragon from the graveyard.
card_roles.Maelstrom of the Spirit Dragon: Any colour for Dragon or Omen spells only, with a late-game sacrifice that tutors any Dragon to hand. Same restriction warning as Haven: spells only, never abilities.
card_roles.Unclaimed Territory: Any colour for creature spells of the chosen type — name Dragons and it fixes everything you actually cast, though the restricted mana pays for spells only.
card_roles.Path of Ancestry: Five-colour fixing that scries every time it casts a Dragon — with 21 Dragon-typed maindeck cards, that is most of your spells. Enters tapped; play it on a quiet turn.
card_roles.Command Tower: The best land in the deck: every commander colour, untapped, no questions.
card_roles.The World Tree: Taps for {G} early; at six lands it turns your entire manabase into any-colour sources — the deck's second Chromatic Lantern. (The God-tutor line is flavour text in a deck with no Gods... except Tiamat, technically a Dragon God, but the ten-mana activation is not a plan.)
card_roles.City of Brass: Any colour for 1 damage per tap — pay the life, cast the Dragon; the deck's life total is a resource its 24 threat bodies defend.
card_roles.Forbidden Orchard: Any colour, and the opponent's 1/1 Spirit is close to irrelevant at a table where your average body is a 5/5 flier.
card_roles.Exotic Orchard: Any colour a rival's lands could make — at a four-player table, nearly always the colour you need.
card_roles.Reflecting Pool: Any type your other lands could produce — with The World Tree online, that is everything.
card_roles.Fabled Passage: Fetches a basic, untapped once you hit four lands; also the shuffle that resets a bad Herald's Horn or Korlessa peek.
card_roles.Jetmir's Garden: A Naya triome with cycling — three colours when you need fixing, a fresh card for {3} when you don't.
card_roles.Ziatora's Proving Ground: The Jund triome, cycling included — and it covers black, the deck's thinnest colour on land sources.
card_roles.Savage Lands: Jund fixing on a budget; enters tapped, so lead with it on turns you're not casting.
card_roles.Canopy Vista: Selesnya battle land — untapped from turn 3 on with two basics down.
card_roles.Cinder Glade: Gruul battle land; same rule — count your basics before sequencing.
card_roles.Blood Crypt: Shock land, Rakdos: pay 2 life for untapped black — the colour deck-facts says the lands are shortest on.
card_roles.Breeding Pool: Shock land, Simic — the untapped {G}/{U} that casts a turn-4 Miirym.
card_roles.Overgrown Tomb: Shock land, Golgari — a Forest for Nature's Lore that also fixes black.
card_roles.Steam Vents: Shock land, Izzet — untapped Izzet mana for counterspell turns.
card_roles.Stomping Ground: Shock land, Gruul — a Nature's Lore-fetchable Forest in the deck's two heaviest colours.
card_roles.Clifftop Retreat: Boros check land — untapped alongside any Mountain or Plains type, which this manabase provides in quantity.
card_roles.Glacial Fortress: Azorius check land for the counterspell colours.
card_roles.Rootbound Crag: Gruul check land — nearly always untapped in a 15-red, 14-green source base.
card_roles.Forest: Four basics anchor the battle lands, Fabled Passage, and Farseek's cousins; green and red carry the deck's heaviest pip load (deck-facts: 23 and 45 total pips), so basics skew accordingly.
card_roles.Mountain: See Forest — the red basic serves the deck's 45 red pips, the heaviest colour ask in the list.
card_roles.Island: The blue basic backs 10 blue land sources for the counterspell suite and Miirym.
card_roles.Swamp: The lone black basic — black has just 11 land sources against Patriarch's Bidding's double-black ask, so guard it.

mulligan: Keep hands with two to four lands and at least one piece of acceleration — and treat cost reducers as the acceleration that matters most. The goldfish run is blunt about this: some ramp or fixing is drawn by turn 6 in 75.6% of games, but a cost reducer in only 42.9%, and the reducers, not the land drops, are what compress a nine-drop curve into a castable one (land drops decay to 50.1% by turn 6). A hand with Dragonspeaker Shaman, Urza's Incubator, or Herald's Horn is a keep almost regardless of what else it holds; the simulator's 'turn-5 Ur-Dragon hand' (reducer plus ramp) assembles by turn 6 in only 29% of games, so when you're dealt one, do not ship it hunting for prettier Dragons. The second thing to want is an early payoff — Dragon Tempest, Garruk's Uprising, Roiling Dragonstorm — because the engine pays per Dragon and wants to be down before the first one lands. What you never mulligan for is the commander: Eminence works from the command zone, so a hand that casts him is worth nothing extra. Ship hands that are all lands and seven-drops with no bridge, and hands whose colours can't cast their spells — five colours is a real tax, black is the thinnest at 11 land sources, and the six spells-only sources (Haven, Maelstrom, Unclaimed Territory, Rivaz, Sarkhan) only count toward casting Dragons, not toward abilities or non-Dragon spells. A protection spell (Teferi's Protection, Heroic Intervention, Flawless Maneuver) is a genuine keep-bonus — held protection is what lets you commit the wave later — and the simulator's 76% keep-7 rate says most sevens are fine; mulligan for function, not for glamour.
upgrades:
The upgrade path lives in the deck's own 38-card sideboard, and the sideboard analysis sorts it cleanly: mostly a bench of interchangeable Dragon bodies plus a spellslinger package that belongs to a different deck, hiding four genuinely differentiated cards. Two are unconditional promotes. Deflecting Swat comes in for An Offer You Can't Refuse: free only while a commander you control is actually on the battlefield — Eminence works from the command zone and does not switch it on, so expect to pay {2}{R} until the turn-nine landing, after which it is free exactly when The Ur-Dragon becomes the table's removal magnet — it retargets the removal aimed at The Ur-Dragon or the counterspell aimed at Tiamat, and it hits abilities, which nothing in the 99 does; the Offer answered the same threats for {U} but handed its controller two Treasures on the way out. Korlessa, Scale Singer comes in for Dragonlord's Servant: with 21 Dragon-typed cards, Path of Ancestry's scry, and Herald's Horn's upkeep peek to rig her top card, a two-mana engine that casts Dragons off the library simply outworks the deck's seventh cost-reduction effect — and she is herself a Dragon for the typal payoffs. Neither swap moves the bracket floor.

The third swap is a dial, not a default: Aggravated Assault in for Crucible of Fire, only at tables that have agreed to bracket 4, because the computed floor moves from 3 to 4 the moment Assault is in the list. The Savage Ventmaw loop it enables is checker-verified (stack 003) — this is a real, unbounded win, not a combo-database rumour — while Crucible's +3/+3 is the right cut because the deck wins on triggers, not on stats. Sneak Attack stays benched by default: against counter-heavy pods it lands Drakuseth without casting, but in normal pods it wastes the Eminence discount the deck is built around. Three sideboard cards — Old Gnawbone, Utvara Hellkite, Encroaching Dragonstorm — are duplicate copies of maindeck cards: spares for wear and foiling, never legal swaps.

One reassurance from the obsolescence index: run against this list, it mostly argues the deck already upgraded itself. Klauth's listed successor is Savage Ventmaw — in the deck. Skyshroud Claim's listed replacements are Farseek and Nature's Lore — in the deck, alongside it, because ramp redundancy is the strategy. Temur Ascendancy's flagged successor is Garruk's Uprising — in the deck, stacked with it, since the draw layer wants both triggers. The index's suggestions for Crux of Fate (Extinction Event and friends) are worth ignoring entirely: none of the listed cards can destroy all non-Dragon creatures while sparing your board, and that one-sided mode is the whole reason Crux holds the slot.
